summary: VFR keeps you in sight of the ground and clear of cloud. Above FL100 you need 8 km visibility, below it 5 km, and 1,500 m horizontally and 1,000 ft vertically from cloud, except in Class F and G at or below 3,000 ft, where clear of cloud with the surface in sight will do (and 1,500 m visibility at 140 kt or less). The UK lets you fly clear of cloud in Class D below 3,000 ft by day at 140 kt or less. A CTR aerodrome needs 5 km and a 1,500 ft ceiling unless you are Special VFR. At night: ceiling 1,500 ft, ground visibility 5 km, 1,000 ft (2,000 ft over high ground) above obstacles within 8 km.
sections: Visual Flight Rules (SERA.5005)
A basic PPL holder (no IR(R) or IR) needs visual reference outside for both attitude and navigation. Losing it, for example by entering cloud or poor visibility, can be disastrous.
The Visual Flight Rules (VFR) set minimum flight visibility and distance from cloud. Conditions that meet them are Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC).
Starting point: flight visibility 8 km, 1,500 m horizontally and 1,000 ft vertically from cloud. Below FL100 the visibility minimum drops to 5 km.
Only two flight categories exist: VFR or IFR.
VMC minima by airspace class (SERA.5001)
At and above 10,000 ft amsl (FL100): Class A B C D E F G; Flight visibility 8 km; Distance from cloud 1,500 m horizontally, 1,000 ft vertically
Below 10,000 ft, above 3,000 ft amsl or 1,000 ft above terrain (whichever is higher): Class A B C D E F G; Flight visibility 5 km; Distance from cloud 1,500 m horizontally, 1,000 ft vertically
At and below 3,000 ft amsl or 1,000 ft above terrain (whichever is higher): Class A B C D E; Flight visibility 5 km; Distance from cloud 1,500 m horizontally, 1,000 ft vertically
At and below 3,000 ft amsl or 1,000 ft above terrain (whichever is higher): Class F G; Flight visibility 5 km (can be less, see below); Distance from cloud Clear of cloud with the surface in sight
Class A minima are guidance only: VFR is not allowed in Class A.
If the transition altitude is lower than 10,000 ft, use FL100 instead of 10,000 ft.

In F and G the visibility may be reduced to 1,500 m when flying at 140 kt IAS or less (time to see and avoid traffic and obstacles), or where meeting other traffic is unlikely. Helicopters may go down to 800 m if flown slowly enough to see and avoid.

UK Class D (at or below 3,000 ft amsl or 1,000 ft above terrain, whichever is higher): you meet SERA.5001 if you fly by day, at 140 kt IAS or less, clear of cloud with the surface in sight, with flight visibility at least 5 km (helicopters 1,500 m).
Note Under VFR the pilot alone is responsible for the safety of the flight, separation from other aircraft, terrain clearance and staying far enough from cloud in adequate visibility.
VFR into a control zone

Unless cleared Special VFR, a VFR flight must not take off or land at an aerodrome in a control zone, or enter its ATZ or circuit, when the reported ground visibility is less than 5 km or the cloud ceiling is less than 1,500 ft.
VFR flight plan and ATC clearance

In Class C and D, the pilot-in-command must give flight details to the ATC unit and get an ATC clearance (the unit may waive this). The details must be enough to issue a clearance and for search and rescue.
Keep a continuous listening watch on the frequency and comply with ATC instructions.
Exemptions (in practice Class D only):
– gliders with 8 km visibility, 1,500 m horizontally and 1,000 ft vertically from cloud
– non-radio powered aircraft by day with 5 km visibility, 1,500 m and 1,000 ft from cloud, with prior ATC permission
Night VFR
Night (ANO): from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, measured at the surface.
Minima for VFR at night:
– cloud ceiling at least 1,500 ft (450 m). The book says "AMSL" in the licences chapter, but a ceiling is measured above ground or water.
– ground visibility at least 5 km
– at or below 3,000 ft amsl (or 1,000 ft above terrain), keep sight of the surface
– except taking off or landing, at least 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km (2,000 ft over high or mountainous terrain)
If leaving the vicinity of the aerodrome, file a flight plan (a full plan or an abbreviated one, i.e. booking out). Establish two-way radio contact.

UK difference (book, licences chapter): you may fly below 1,000 ft above obstacles within 8 km if you stay at or below 3,000 ft amsl, clear of cloud with the surface in sight, and still meet the low-flying rules (1,000 ft over congested areas within 600 m or glide clear; 500 ft from the ground elsewhere).
Notes on VFR
Always fly within the privileges of your licence (a basic PPL, for example, has no IMC privileges).
Using semicircular cruising levels is advised even under VFR, though flying on the Regional Pressure Setting above 3,000 ft is fine, especially when manoeuvring.

sum.Visual Flight Rules (SERA.5005): VFR sets minimum visibility and distance from cloud; meeting them is VMC. The baseline is 8 km, 1,500 m and 1,000 ft.
sum.VMC minima by airspace class (SERA.5001): 5 km below FL100 (8 km above); 1,500 m and 1,000 ft from cloud, except F and G low down: clear of cloud, surface in sight.
sum.VFR into a control zone: No VFR take-off, landing or circuit at a CTR aerodrome below 5 km ground visibility or a 1,500 ft ceiling, unless Special VFR.
sum.VFR flight plan and ATC clearance: In Class C and D, give flight details, get a clearance, listen out and obey ATC.
sum.Night VFR: Night is 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise; ceiling 1,500 ft, 5 km, and 1,000 ft above obstacles within 8 km.
sum.Notes on VFR: Stay within your licence privileges; semicircular levels are advised, but QNH/RPS is fine above 3,000 ft.

cards.q: VFR flight visibility at and above FL100?
Class F/G at or below 3,000 ft amsl (or 1,000 ft agl if higher)?
cards.a: 5 km, clear of cloud with the surface in sight.

cards.q: When can Class G visibility drop to 1,500 m?
cards.a: At or below 3,000 ft at 140 kt IAS or less (or where traffic is unlikely).

cards.q: UK Class D alleviation below 3,000 ft?
cards.a: By day, 140 kt IAS or less, clear of cloud with the surface in sight, 5 km visibility.

cards.q: Is VFR allowed in Class A?
cards.a: No. Its VMC minima are guidance only.

cards.q: VFR into a CTR aerodrome: minimum ground visibility and ceiling?
cards.a: 5 km and 1,500 ft, unless cleared Special VFR.
From 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise, at the surface.
1,500 ft (450 m), measured above the ground.

cards.q: Night VFR minimum height en route?
cards.a: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km (2,000 ft over high terrain).

cards.q: Who keeps a VFR flight separated from other aircraft?
What two things do Class C and D need from a VFR flight?
cards.a: Flight details to ATC and an ATC clearance (plus a listening watch).

quiz.q: Between FL100 and 3,000 ft amsl in Class E, the VFR minima are:
o: 5 km, 1,500 m horizontally and 1,000 ft vertically from cloud
8 km, 1,500 m horizontally and 1,000 ft vertically from cloud
5 km, 1,000 m horizontally and 1,500 ft vertically from cloud
5 km, clear of cloud and in sight of the surface
quiz.why: Below FL100 visibility drops to 5 km but the cloud distances stay 1,500 m and 1,000 ft. 8 km applies only at and above FL100, and the 1,000 m / 1,500 ft pair has the numbers swapped.

quiz.q: At 2,000 ft amsl in Class G by day at 120 kt, the lowest flight visibility allowed under VFR is:
o: 1,500 m, clear of cloud with the surface in sight
5 km, clear of cloud with the surface in sight
1,500 m, 1,000 ft vertically from cloud
800 m, clear of cloud
quiz.why: In F and G at or below 3,000 ft the minimum is 5 km, but it may be 1,500 m at 140 kt IAS or less. Cloud distance is clear of cloud with the surface in sight; 800 m is for helicopters.

quiz.q: The UK Class D alleviation (clear of cloud, surface in sight) applies:
o: By day, at 140 kt IAS or less, at or below 3,000 ft amsl (or 1,000 ft above terrain if higher)
By day or night, at 140 kt IAS or less, at or below 3,000 ft amsl
By day, at any speed, at or below 3,000 ft amsl
By day, at 140 kt IAS or less, at or below FL100
quiz.why: All three conditions together: day, 140 kt or less, and at or below 3,000 ft amsl or 1,000 ft above terrain, with 5 km visibility.

quiz.q: Unless cleared Special VFR, you may not take off from an aerodrome in a CTR under VFR when:
o: The ground visibility is below 5 km or the cloud ceiling below 1,500 ft
The flight visibility is below 8 km or the ceiling below 1,500 ft
The ground visibility is below 5 km or the ceiling below 1,000 ft
The ground visibility is below 1,500 m or the ceiling below 1,500 ft
quiz.why: 5 km ground visibility and a 1,500 ft ceiling. It is reported ground visibility, not flight visibility.

quiz.q: For night VFR, the cloud ceiling must be at least:
o: 1,500 ft above the ground
1,500 ft amsl
1,000 ft above the ground
2,000 ft above the ground
quiz.why: 450 m (1,500 ft). A ceiling is always measured above ground or water, so 'amsl' is the trap.

quiz.q: Except taking off or landing, a night VFR flight over ordinary terrain must stay at least:
o: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km
1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 nm
1,500 ft above the highest obstacle within 5 km
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 150 m
quiz.why: 1,000 ft within 8 km (2,000 ft over high or mountainous terrain). 8 nm is the wrong unit; 500 ft within 150 m is the day low-flying rule.

quiz.q: Under VFR, who is responsible for separation from other aircraft and terrain?
o: The pilot alone
ATC in controlled airspace, the pilot elsewhere
The pilot, but ATC in Class C and D
ATC whenever the aircraft has a clearance
quiz.why: Under VFR the pilot is solely responsible for separation, terrain clearance and staying in VMC, even with a clearance.

quiz.q: A VFR flight into Class D must:
o: Give flight details to ATC, get a clearance, listen out and comply with instructions
Book out only; no clearance is needed
File a full flight plan at least 60 minutes before departure
Have a transponder with Mode S
quiz.why: Class C and D need flight details and a clearance, plus a listening watch. An abbreviated plan by radio is enough.
